n: The villain enters. Haman is promoted to the highest position in the empire. He is called an Agagite — recalling Agag, king of the Amalekites, Israel’s ancient enemy whom Saul (a Benjamite like Mordecai) failed to destroy.

f.w: set his seat above all the princes
f.g: Made him prime minister, second only to the king.

n: Everyone at the gate bows to Haman as the king ordered — except Mordecai. Bowing as a courtesy wasn’t forbidden to Jews, so Mordecai’s refusal seems tied to who Haman was, or to Haman claiming more honor than was right.
The other officials ask Mordecai why he is disobeying the king’s command.
After days of refusal, they report him to Haman to see whether his excuse — that he was a Jew — would hold. Mordecai’s identity is now known.

f.g: Whether his reason would be accepted.

f.w: he had told them that he was a Jew

n: When Haman sees it for himself, he is filled with rage. His pride cannot bear one man’s refusal to honor him.
Punishing Mordecai alone seems too small to Haman. He decides to wipe out every Jew in the empire. Wounded pride grows into plans for genocide.

f.g: Thought it beneath him, too small a revenge.

f.w: sought to destroy all the Jews

n: Five years after Esther became queen, Haman casts lots, called “Pur,” to choose a lucky day for the slaughter. The lot falls almost a year away — giving God’s plan time to unfold. The feast of Purim takes its name from this word.

f.g: An Akkadian (Babylonian) word for a lot, like dice; plural Purim (Esther 9:24-26).
The first month, roughly March–April; Passover month.

n: Haman’s pitch to the king is a classic piece of prejudice: a scattered people with different customs who supposedly don’t obey the king’s laws. He never names them, mixing half-truths with lies.

f.w: their laws are diverse from all people
f.g: Their customs differ — they worship one God and keep the Sabbath and dietary laws.
Tolerate them, allow them to live.

n: He asks for a decree to destroy them and offers an enormous bribe — possibly two-thirds of the empire’s yearly income — perhaps hoping to pay it from the plunder.

f.g: Roughly 375 tons of silver — a staggering sum.

n: Without even asking who the people are, the king hands Haman his signet ring — full authority to issue laws in the king’s name. Haman is now openly called “the Jews’ enemy.”

f.g: The signet ring used to seal royal decrees, giving them the king’s authority.

n: The king tells Haman to keep his money and do as he likes with the people. Whether the king declines the money or is being polite is unclear; either way, he gives up a whole people carelessly.

f.w: The silver is given to thee
f.g: Possibly a polite formula; Esther 4:7 suggests the money was still expected.

n: On the thirteenth of Nisan — the eve of Passover, when Jews remembered God’s deliverance from Egypt — scribes write the decree in every language and seal it with the king’s ring.

f.w: the thirteenth day of the first month

n: Couriers carry the order everywhere: on a single day, the thirteenth of Adar, kill every Jew — young and old, women and children — and seize their property.

f.g: Couriers on fast horses; the Persian royal road system was famous for its speed.

f.w: to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish
f.g: A triple phrase stressing total destruction.

n: A copy is posted publicly in every province so that enemies of the Jews could prepare for that day.
The couriers rush off. The king and Haman sit down to drink, unconcerned, while the city of Susa is thrown into confusion and dismay. Many ordinary people sensed the injustice.

f.w: the king and Haman sat down to drink
